clue.text: "Twas my one Glory - / Let it be / - / I was owned of Thee -" (Emily Dickinson)

definitions.text: "Twas my one Glory - / Let it be / - / I was owned of Thee -" (Emily Dickinson)

parts.words: "Twas my one Glory - / Let it be / - / I was owned of Thee -" (Emily Dickinson)
parts.note: a quotation from an Emily Dickinson poem with one word blanked out; the missing word, which completes 'Let it be ___', is the entry

explanation.surface: A fragment of Emily Dickinson's verse about the glory of belonging to a beloved.
explanation.walkthrough: This is a fill-in-the-blank quotation clue, a TLS speciality: there is no wordplay, only literary knowledge of the line 'Let it be ___ / I was owned of Thee'.
explanation.definitionFit: The poem's line reads that the speaker's glory should be kept in memory, so the gap takes the past participle for being recalled.

clue.text: Are you texting dates for Queensland writer?

parts.note: in text-message spelling 'are' is written as the single letter R
in text-message spelling 'you' is written as the single letter U
D is an abbreviation for date, doubled for the plural

explanation.surface: Someone asks, in a phone message, which dates suit a writer from Queensland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'texting' tells you to use text-speak: R for 'are', U for 'you'. Steele Rudd was the pen name of the Queensland author of the Dad and Dave stories.
explanation.definitionFit: Steele Rudd, pen name of Arthur Hoey Davis, was an author born and working in Queensland, Australia.

clue.text: Knight being carried by pram or dredger

indicators.note: something carried by these words sits inside them, so the entry is a run of letters inside 'pram or dredger'

explanation.surface: A knight is transported in a baby carriage or a dredging boat.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across 'praM OR DREDger'. Mordred is the treacherous knight of Arthurian legend.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Mordred is one of the Knights of the Round Table, who betrays King Arthur.

clue.text: Great works in museum pong as rotten

indicators.note: something rotten has broken down, so these letters are broken up and reassembled

explanation.surface: Masterpieces in a museum that smells, as if they are decaying.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rotten' reworks the twelve letters of MUSEUM PONG AS into the plural of the Latin phrase for an artist's chief work.
explanation.definitionFit: A magnum opus is a writer's or artist's greatest achievement, Latin for 'great work'.

clue.text: Son hugged by public schoolboy Toomas Nipernaadi?

indicators.note: a thing hugged by another is held inside it, so the first piece goes within the second

parts.note: an Etonian is a pupil of Eton College, the famous English public (fee-paying) school

explanation.surface: A boy at an English public school embraces his son, a character called Toomas Nipernaadi.
explanation.walkthrough: Toomas Nipernaadi is the vagabond hero of August Gailit's novel; the question mark marks him as an example of a national of his country. In Britain a 'public school' is an elite private school.
explanation.definitionFit: Toomas Nipernaadi is a famous character of Baltic literature, a citizen of the country whose capital is Tallinn.

clue.text: Incense nurse put by kid close to Rosaline

parts.note: EN stands for Enrolled Nurse, a crossword staple
to kid is to tease, which is to rag someone

indicators.note: the close of a word is its final letter, here taken from Rosaline

explanation.surface: A nurse beside a child annoys someone near Rosaline, perhaps in a Shakespeare play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Incense' is the verb (stressed on the second syllable), meaning to make furious, not the fragrant smoke. 'put by' just places the pieces side by side.
explanation.definitionFit: To incense someone is to infuriate them, making them very angry.

clue.text: Hobo visited by a Bancroft, Staunton, and Van Dyne?

indicators.note: a place visited by someone has that person inside it, so the A goes within the other piece

parts.note: a hobo is a tramp or vagrant, in American English a bum

explanation.surface: A tramp receives visitors with the surnames Bancroft, Staunton and Van Dyne.
explanation.walkthrough: L. Frank Baum, author of The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, also wrote as Laura Bancroft, Schuyler Staunton and Edith Van Dyne; the question mark flags that these are pseudonyms.
explanation.definitionFit: The Oz author published books under the pen names Laura Bancroft, Schuyler Staunton and Edith Van Dyne, so each was really him.

clue.text: Royal men appearing in a paper with knight

indicators.note: the men appear inside the other letters, so they are placed within them

parts.note: a rag is slang for a low-quality newspaper
N is the chess notation for a knight
OR stands for Other Ranks, soldiers who are not officers

explanation.surface: Members of a royal household feature in a newspaper alongside a knight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Royal' looks like an adjective qualifying 'men', but it is a noun definition: Aragorn is the heir to the throne of Gondor in Tolkien's The Lord of the Rings.
explanation.definitionFit: Tolkien's ranger turns out to be the rightful king of Gondor, a royal personage.

clue.text: "Five miles — with a mazy motion / Through wood and dale the sacred river ran" (Samuel Taylor Coleridge)

definitions.text: "Five miles — with a mazy motion / Through wood and dale the sacred river ran" (Samuel Taylor Coleridge)

parts.words: "Five miles — with a mazy motion / Through wood and dale the sacred river ran" (Samuel Taylor Coleridge)
parts.note: a line from Coleridge's Kubla Khan with one word blanked out after 'Five miles'; the missing word describing the river's winding course is the entry

explanation.surface: Coleridge's description of the sacred river Alph winding through Xanadu.
explanation.walkthrough: A fill-in-the-blank quotation: Kubla Khan reads 'Five miles ___ with a mazy motion'. The gap is marked by the dash.
explanation.definitionFit: The river follows a winding, wandering course, which the gap word describes as a present participle.

clue.text: Move socialist backed a conservative finds offensive

indicators.note: turned to face backwards, so the move and the socialist are read in reverse together

parts.note: to go is to move
a red is a left-winger or socialist
a Tory is a member of the UK Conservative Party

explanation.surface: A conservative judges a socialist's proposal to be offensive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backed' reverses GO + RED as a block to give DEROG; then add A and TORY. 'finds' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Derogatory remarks belittle or insult, so they are offensive.

clue.text: Cut the first two slices of fruit tart

indicators.text: Cut the first two slices of
indicators.note: the first two letters of the fruit's name are removed, as if two slices were cut off its front

parts.note: a banana is a fruit

explanation.surface: Instructions to trim two slices off some fruit for a dessert tart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tart' is not a pastry: Nana is the courtesan heroine of Zola's novel of that name, so she is a tart in the old slang sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Zola's Nana is a courtesan, and a courtesan or prostitute is called a tart in slang.

clue.text: American locked in loft with singer and lawyer

indicators.note: the American is shut up in the loft, so that piece follows directly after it

parts.note: a loft is an attic, the room under a roof
US stands for United States, so American
a finch is a songbird

explanation.surface: An American shut in an attic with a songbird and a lawyer.
explanation.walkthrough: Atticus Finch is the lawyer in Harper Lee's To Kill a Mockingbird, which suits the bird-themed surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Atticus Finch defends Tom Robinson in court in To Kill a Mockingbird, a famous fictional attorney.

clue.text: Thomas Mann's missus is endlessly cheating

indicators.note: without its end, so the final letter is dropped

parts.note: fraud is cheating or deception

explanation.surface: Thomas Mann's wife is accused of being unfaithful without end.
explanation.walkthrough: Frau is the German for wife or Mrs, apt for the German novelist Thomas Mann.
explanation.definitionFit: German Frau means wife or Mrs, so it is what a German such as Mann would call his missus.

clue.text: Soon time to get deal, perhaps, for Barnes book

parts.note: nigh means near, so soon
deal is a kind of softwood timber, so an example of wood

explanation.surface: Soon it will be time to complete a deal for a book by Barnes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'deal' here is pine or fir timber, not a bargain. Nightwood is the 1936 novel by Djuna Barnes.
explanation.definitionFit: Nightwood is the best-known novel of the American modernist writer Djuna Barnes.

clue.text: This dim ode upset one who wrote about dogs

indicators.note: upset means knocked over, so these letters are thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: A dull poem distresses a canine author.
explanation.walkthrough: Dodie Smith wrote The Hundred and One Dalmatians.
explanation.definitionFit: Dodie Smith is the novelist of The Hundred and One Dalmatians, a story of a canine family.

clue.text: Miss Marple is one cautious person

definitions.meaning: Agatha Christie's elderly amateur sleuth is an elderly spinster
a fussy, timid person of either sex is disparagingly called this

explanation.surface: Agatha Christie's sleuth is described as a careful type.
explanation.walkthrough: Two definitions: Miss Marple is literally an elderly lady, and the same phrase is slang for a timid, fussy person.
explanation.definitionFit: Miss Marple is an elderly spinster, and the phrase is also used figuratively for any overcautious worrier.

clue.text: You might say Adam Smith's foremost secret

indicators.note: the foremost part of a word is its first letter, here of Smith's

parts.note: inner thoughts are private or secret ones

explanation.surface: A suggestion that the economist Adam Smith's chief secret is being revealed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Adam Smith' looks like the economist, but 'Adam' alone is the definition: the first man, who ate the forbidden fruit, is the archetypal wrongdoer.
explanation.definitionFit: Adam disobeyed God in Eden, so he is the first transgressor in the Bible; 'You might say' signals an example.

clue.text: Metrical analysis of first in Shakespeare's canon is duff

indicators.note: the first letter of Shakespeare's is taken
duff means faulty or useless, so the letters of 'canon is' are rearranged

explanation.surface: An analysis of the metre of the opening of Shakespeare's works is poor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'duff' is British slang for bad or broken. The surface suggests a poor reading of Shakespeare; the definition sits at the front, as the name of the analysis itself.
explanation.definitionFit: Scansion is the analysis of verse into metrical feet and stresses.

clue.text: Self motors around university to see high-flyer

parts.note: I is the first-person pronoun, oneself

indicators.note: the cars are placed around the university letter

parts.note: motors are cars

explanation.surface: A person drives round a campus to look at a high achiever.
explanation.walkthrough: Icarus flew too near the sun on wax wings, so he is literally a high-flyer.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth Icarus flew so close to the sun that his wings melted, a literal soarer.

clue.text: A Verne novel about good guy like Macduff?

indicators.note: the rearranged letters go about, that is around, the G
novel as an adjective means new, so the letters of 'A Verne' are made anew

explanation.surface: A Jules Verne novel about a good man resembling Macduff.
explanation.walkthrough: 'novel' looks like a book by Verne but is the anagram signal. Macduff kills Macbeth to avenge his murdered family.
explanation.definitionFit: Macduff kills Macbeth in revenge for the slaughter of his wife and children, so he takes vengeance.

clue.text: Symphonic composer (Germanic), creator of Oxford?

definitions.meaning: Robert ..., the German Romantic composer, wrote four symphonies
an Oxford is a style of shoe, and German Schuhmann means shoemaker, so its maker in German terms

explanation.surface: A German composer of symphonies is credited with founding Oxford.
explanation.walkthrough: Oxford is not the city or university but the lace-up shoe; in German a shoemaker is a Schuhmann, close to the composer's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Robert Schumann composed four symphonies; his surname also echoes German for a cobbler, one who makes brogues and similar footwear.

clue.text: Bit of residue in unopened port makes you more mad

indicators.note: the bit of residue goes inside the shortened port
with its opening letter removed

parts.note: Tangier is a Moroccan port

indicators.note: a small bit of residue is its first letter

explanation.surface: Finding some residue in a bottle of port that has not been opened makes you more angry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'port' is the city of Tangier, not the wine: 'unopened' removes its T to leave ANGIER, and R goes inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Angry means mad in the sense of furious, so the comparative is more mad.

clue.text: One publishing children's author's last piece

parts.note: issue means offspring or children

indicators.note: the last letter of author's is taken, ignoring the possessive

explanation.surface: Someone publishes the final work of a children's writer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'children's author' looks like a writer of children's books; split it into 'children' (ISSUE) and the last letter of 'author'.
explanation.definitionFit: To issue a book is to publish it, so one who does that is a publisher.

clue.text: St Ives writer's flat lad found on side of street

indicators.note: the sides of a word are its first and last letters, here of street

parts.note: even means level or flat
a son is a lad

explanation.surface: A writer from the Cornish town of St Ives finds a boy's flat on a street.
explanation.walkthrough: St Ives is not the Cornish resort but Robert Louis Stevenson's novel St. Ives. The first and last letters of 'street' give ST.
explanation.definitionFit: Robert Louis Stevenson wrote the novel St. Ives, about a French prisoner escaping in Scotland.

clue.text: Better get good offices for leaders after revolution

indicators.note: after being turned round, the picked letters are read backwards
the leaders of words are their first letters

explanation.surface: Someone advises getting good offices for company leaders after a revolution.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Better' is not 'improve' but a bettor: Phileas Fogg goes round the world in eighty days to win a wager.
explanation.definitionFit: Phileas Fogg in Verne's Around the World in Eighty Days makes a wager, so he is a gambler.

clue.text: Alec Leamas is one seen by English spot

parts.note: Alec Leamas is the agent in le Carré's The Spy Who Came in from the Cold

explanation.surface: Le Carré's agent Alec Leamas is noticed by an Englishman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spot' is the verb, to catch sight of.
explanation.definitionFit: To espy something is to catch sight of or notice it.

clue.text: I stab when meeting Emilia finally

definitions.text: I stab when meeting Emilia finally

parts.note: to have a stab is to have a go, so 'stab' gives A GO

explanation.surface: A villain confesses to stabbing when he finally confronts Emilia.
explanation.walkthrough: In Othello, Iago stabs his wife Emilia at the end of the play, so the whole clue describes him.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's villain kills Emilia, his own wife, in the final scene of Othello.

clue.text: Is journal roughly about one who wrote of loves that bind?

definitions.text: who wrote of loves that bind

indicators.note: the rearranged letters go about the single letter
roughly means approximately, so the letters are only roughly in order and must be rearranged

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A journal looks at an author who wrote about binding love.
explanation.walkthrough: Julián Ríos is the Spanish novelist whose book Loves That Bind was translated into English.
explanation.definitionFit: The Spanish novelist Julián Ríos wrote Amores que atan, translated as Loves That Bind.

clue.text: Lamp-lighter in house is European queen

indicators.note: the letters for European queen go inside the house abbreviation

parts.note: R stands for Regina, Latin for queen

explanation.surface: A European queen in a house is the one who lights the lamps.
explanation.walkthrough: In Greek legend Hero lit a lamp in her tower each night to guide Leander across the Hellespont.
explanation.definitionFit: In the myth, Hero lit a lamp nightly to guide her lover Leander as he swam to her.

clue.text: Young detective writer on the tail of Blunt

indicators.note: the writer comes on the tail of, that is after, the blunt piece

parts.note: blunt means outspoken, or frank
Thomas Hardy, the English novelist

explanation.surface: A youthful sleuth follows the writer Blunt closely.
explanation.walkthrough: Frank Hardy is one of the Hardy Boys, the teenage detectives of American juvenile fiction.
explanation.definitionFit: Frank Hardy is one of the teenage brothers who solve mysteries in the Hardy Boys books.
